name: German Volume Training
author: from Rolf Feser; made known by Charles Poliquin
structure: One big exercise for a body part done for ten sets of ten, starting at about 60 % of a max with about a minute's rest, and a little accessory work after it.
progression: When all ten sets reach ten reps, add 4-5 % next time; until then the load stays.
adapt: Written as a cycle, the load is held until all ten sets reach ten reps and then raised, as the method has it. The one-minute rest is advice; the plan does not carry rest times.
caveats: A short push for size: very high volume and little strength gain. Only the outline was checked.

name: Super Squats (20-rep squat)
author: Randall Strossen; the method goes back to Peary Rader and others
structure: One set of twenty squats with a ten-rep-max load, breathing between reps, three times a week, with a few basic upper-body lifts.
progression: At least 2.5 kg (5 lb) more on the squat every session for six weeks, with no rule for a miss, and then it ends.
adapt: Written as a six-week cycle with the squat load rising every session; the three days are three routines when their loads differ. A run of misses means the programme is over, by its own rules.
caveats: Known for how hard it is. The book's claim of 30 lb of muscle in six weeks is not realistic. Only the outline was checked.

name: Reg Park 5x5
author: Reg Park (1960)
structure: Phase one: squat, bench press and deadlift three times a week for five sets of five, of which the first two are ramping warm-ups and three are at the working load, with three to five minutes' rest. Two later phases add exercises.
progression: When all three working sets reach five reps, add load.
adapt: Plan the three working sets as 3x5; the two ramping sets are warm-ups, which the plan does not hold. Phases two and three are new plans, asked for when the first has run.
caveats: One of the first 5x5 programmes. Deadlifting for working sets three times a week is hard to recover from. Only the outline was checked.

name: DoggCrapp (DC Training)
author: Dante Trudel
structure: Two alternating sessions, with three exercises kept in rotation for every body part and one rest-pause set of each: three short bouts for 11-15 reps in all, then loaded stretching.
progression: Every session has to beat the log; past the top of the rep range the load goes up. An exercise that cannot be beaten twice running is replaced. Six to twelve weeks of this, then ten to fourteen days of easy training.
adapt: A rest-pause set is not something the plan can prescribe, and three exercises rotating for each body part would need the plan rewritten every session.
caveats: Short and frequent. Every set goes to failure, which is hard on the joints and the head. Not for newer lifters.

name: Mike Mentzer Heavy Duty (HIT)
author: Mike Mentzer, after Arthur Jones
structure: One or two warm-up sets and then a single set to failure of 6-10 reps for each exercise, often as a pre-exhaust superset of an isolation lift into a compound one. About three sessions a week, further apart as recovery asks.
progression: At the top of the rep range, add load. Two or three sessions without progress add rest days rather than taking load off.
adapt: One set on `double` over 6-10 reps, with pre-exhaust pairs as supersets (`sg`). After repeated misses the app takes about 10 % off where the method adds rest days; spacing the sessions further apart is a change to the week.
caveats: Quick and intense. It runs against the evidence that links volume to growth and is disputed. Only the outline was checked.

name: Mike Mentzer Consolidated Routine
author: Mike Mentzer, Heavy Duty II
structure: Two compound lifts a session, one set to failure each, once every four to seven days.
progression: As Heavy Duty; a stall stretches the days between sessions further.
adapt: The plan can hold the two lifts for one set on `double`. A gap between sessions that keeps growing is not something a weekly schedule can express.
caveats: Extremely low volume, nearer to maintenance than to a programme. Only the outline was checked.

name: Deep Water
author: Jon Andersen
structure: Ten sets of ten of a main lift (squat, deadlift, push press) at 70 % of a ten-rep max, four days a week and a day of active recovery. Beginner, intermediate and advanced phases of six weeks each.
progression: Density first: the load stays while rest falls from four minutes to three to two over six weeks. The next phase raises the load to 80 % and asks for the hundred reps in nine sets, then eight.
adapt: It progresses by shortening rest and by doing the same reps in fewer sets. The plan carries no rest times and the app has no rule of that kind.
caveats: Well regarded for gaining weight and for grit. Sessions of 90-120 minutes, with very high demands on recovery and eating.

name: Gironda 8x8
author: Vince Gironda
structure: Eight sets of eight of every exercise with only about 30 seconds' rest, starting at about 40-50 % of a max.
progression: When all eight sets are complete, a small step up in load or a shorter rest.
adapt: The plan can hold eight sets of eight on `linear`. The 30-second rest, which is the point of the method, is advice only: the plan carries no rest times.
caveats: An old contest-preparation method with very light loads; not for someone after strength. Only its existence and outline are confirmed.
